body.text: On November 5, The Diplomat published an article purporting to quote the CEO of Newtype on his company’s interactions with Ukrainian partners. The author presented themselves as a South Korean freelance journalist and claimed to have interviewed Newtype’s CEO. We now know that the journalist fabricated the interview and may not even be who they claimed to be. Additional scrutiny of the exchange between the journalist and The Diplomat revealed evidence that the emails likely originated in Russia, suggesting this article was part of a disinformation operation.

Newtype is the first South Korean defense start-up to work on the ground in Ukraine. The Diplomat interviewed Sengwon “Joe” Cho, the CEO of Newtype, via email about the fabricated interview, his company’s role in Ukraine, and the future of Newtype’s defense cooperation in Europe.

“Our work in Ukraine continues as planned,” Cho emphasized. “A diplomatic row stopping our work was exactly the false claim in the fabricated article. What I do see is that our adversaries are trying to use the diplomatic differences between Ukraine and South Korea to drive our two countries apart.”
What is the current state of Newtype’s activities in Ukraine?
Our cooperation with Ukraine has not ended, and our testing was never suspended. The quote attributed to me was fabricated. I was never interviewed by the author, and I never said those words.

I can’t disclose details of our activities in Ukraine, only that they are ongoing and that we work closely with our partner, Reaktion Group, which has a team on the ground in Kyiv and team members who regularly go to the front line. It is important for us to learn from Ukraine, and it is an honor for us to support the country.
Why did you seek out cooperation with Ukraine in the first place?

For us, it is all about getting real data. In Korea, startups and even the largest companies want to lead in defense AI, but most of them are building it without ever testing it on the battlefield. During my 12 years as an artillery officer in the Korean Army, I was tired of doing things that had no connection to reality. So as soon as I started this company, I knew Ukraine was the place to start. A system like ours only proves itself when soldiers use it under real pressure, and no one has more recent combat experience in artillery than Ukrainian soldiers. Their feedback is the most valuable thing a company like ours can receive.

Newtype develops AI-enabled defense software for tactical fire command and target processing, based on voice recognition. Our mission is to make the call-for-fire process as efficient as possible, for example when a soldier needs to keep eyes on the target, or when the cold makes it hard to use a tablet.

Above all, Ukrainians are defending their homeland on the front line of the free nations. As a former artillery officer, it is an honor for me to help them. And as a Korean, I know all too well what it feels like to have your country invaded.
Newtype is the first Korean defense startup to conduct tests in Ukraine. Was it difficult to build those relationships, since you were pioneering a new form of cooperation?

Yes. There was no playbook for a Korean defense startup in Ukraine, so we had to build trust step by step. What made it possible was working with a trusted and capable partner, Reaktion Group, and starting by listening to what Ukrainian units actually need instead of just pitching a product.
Has the recent diplomatic tension between the South Korean and Ukrainian governments impacted your company?

No. Our work in Ukraine continues as planned. A diplomatic row stopping our work was exactly the false claim in the fabricated article. What I do see is that our adversaries are trying to use the diplomatic differences between Ukraine and South Korea to drive our two countries apart. I hope their efforts will do the exact opposite, and that we will see more cooperation between my country and Ukraine in the future.
In many ways, Ukraine and South Korea face the same enemies. They have a lot in common, and could learn and benefit a lot from one another.
Why do you think Newtype was targeted for a disinformation operation?

From my perspective, Russia and North Korea are trying to take advantage of the diplomatic differences between Ukraine and South Korea. North Korea is sending soldiers to Russia, and Russia is sending defense technology to North Korea. Both countries have a natural interest in preventing deeper ties between Ukraine and South Korea. As the first Korean defense startup active in Ukraine, we were an obvious target, even though we are a small company. Your own team’s review found that the journalist’s emails came from Russia, which supports this.

This incident also tells me that Russia has noticed our system and wants it gone from the battlefield. They hit us in the information space for the same reason they hit Ukrainian military infrastructure with drones and missiles: to take away tools that would otherwise be used against Russian troops at the front. That shows how much of a threat they consider BARBARA, Newtype’s solution, to be. They want to make sure the Ukrainian Armed Forces cannot use it.
Has Newtype faced other attempts to disrupt its work in Ukraine?

Not that we can discuss publicly. Like any company working in this field, we take security seriously. Our partner Reaktion Group has procedures in place for incidents like this, and we work closely with them.
Do you see scope for expanded cooperation with Ukraine, and perhaps elsewhere in Europe?

Yes. I spoke at at Land Warfare Europe in Vilnius on November 17, and will speak at the UK-UA Defence Tech Forum at RUSI in London on November 20. In Finland, we attended Slush (November 18-19) and had conversations with the defense community. Ukraine remains at the center of our work in Europe, and we see the Nordic and Baltic countries, which face a similar threat, as natural partners.
